questions.q: What does a circuit's width measure?
options: The number of qubits (wires) the circuit uses
The total number of gates anywhere in the circuit
The longest chain of sequentially-dependent gates
The number of measurement operations in the circuit
questions.explain: Width counts qubits/wires, not gates or layers. A circuit with width 5 needs a device with at least 5 physical qubits available, regardless of how many gates it contains.

questions.q: Two gates can be placed in the same depth layer exactly when:
options: They act on completely disjoint sets of qubits, with no shared control or target
They are both single-qubit gates, regardless of which qubits they touch
They both appear earlier than any CNOT gate in the circuit
They use the same gate type, such as two H gates anywhere in the circuit
questions.explain: A layer groups gates that can run in parallel because none of them depend on each other's output. That requires disjoint qubits — if two gates share any qubit, the one applied later necessarily depends on the earlier one having already executed on that qubit.

questions.q: For the worked circuit (H on q1, H on q2 in the same layer, then CNOT with control q1/target q2, qubit 3 unused), what are the width and depth?
options: Width 3, depth 2
Width 2, depth 2
Width 3, depth 3
Width 2, depth 1
questions.explain: Width counts all 3 wires, including idle qubit 3. Depth is 2: the two H gates share layer 1 (disjoint qubits), but the CNOT depends on both post-H states and must be layer 2.

questions.q: Why can't the CNOT in the worked example share a layer with either of the H gates?
options: Because CNOT acts on both q1 and q2, and it needs each qubit's state after that qubit's H gate has already been applied — so it necessarily depends on both H gates finishing first
Because CNOT gates are always defined to be the final gate in any circuit
Because H and CNOT are different gate types and different gate types can never share a layer
Because qubit 3 being idle forces every other gate into a separate layer
questions.explain: The rule is about shared qubits and dependency, not gate type. CNOT touches q1 and q2, both of which already have pending H gates, so CNOT must wait for those to complete — forcing it into a later layer.

questions.q: Why does depth specifically (more than total gate count) matter most on real noisy hardware?
options: Each sequential layer takes real execution time, during which decoherence and gate errors accumulate, so a larger depth means more accumulated noise before the circuit finishes — even if two circuits have the same total gate count
Depth determines how many qubits a device needs, which is the only cost that matters on real hardware
Total gate count is actually irrelevant to performance, while depth is the only cost tracked by any metric
Depth has no physical meaning; it only matters for drawing the diagram neatly
questions.explain: Width sets the qubit-count requirement, but depth sets how long the circuit is physically exposed to decoherence and error-prone gate execution — two circuits with identical gate counts but different depths (because of different parallelism) accumulate different amounts of real-hardware error.
